titulo: How to Reduce Risks of Bad Air Quality

fuente.nota: Text shortened by removing paragraphs; the sentences are unchanged.

parrafos: Air quality differs from place to place and day to day. But about 99 percent of the world’s population breathes air at some point that does not meet pollution guidelines set by the World Health Organization (WHO).

Different forms of air pollution kill about 7 million people each year, the U.N. health agency estimates. But health experts say there are some actions individuals can take to protect themselves, even in the world’s most polluted cities.

The first step is to start with the understanding that air is not only polluted when it looks smoky or smoggy, said Tanushree Ganguly. She is an air quality expert with the Energy Policy Institute of Chicago’s India program.
Air pollutants often come from people burning things. Examples include fuels as well as clearing operations involving crops or trees. Pollutants can also be released from wildfires.

Among the most dangerous particles we can breathe in are called particulate matter. The smallest of these are known as PM 2.5. This is because they are less than 2.5 microns in diameter. These particles can travel deep inside human lungs and are mostly created by burning fuels. Larger particles, known as PM 10, are linked to agriculture, roadways, mining or wind-blown dust.

Other dangerous pollutants include gases like nitrogen dioxide or sulfur dioxide, which are also produced from burning fuels. This information comes from Anumita Roychowdhury, an air pollution expert at the Center for Science and Environment in New Delhi.

Short-term exposure can cause asthma attacks and increase the risk of heart attacks and stroke, especially in older people and those with existing medical problems. Long-term exposure can cause serious heart and lung problems that can lead to death.

A recent study by the U.N. children’s agency UNICEF found that more than 500 million children in East Asia and Pacific countries breathe unhealthy air. The pollution is linked to the deaths of 100 children under age 5 every day. June Kunugi, UNICEF’s Regional Director for East Asia, said the polluted air limits growth, harms lungs and affects thinking abilities.

Over 6,000 cities in 117 countries now record and follow air quality levels. Many mobile apps include air quality information as well. But it can be difficult to know how bad the air is by looking at these numbers.
To help people better understand air quality levels, many countries have established an air quality index, or AQI. Larger numbers on this index mean worse air.
Different countries have different air quality standards. For example, India’s daily PM 2.5 limit is more than 1.5 times higher than in Thailand and 4 times higher than WHO standards.

For individuals, experts say the goal should be to limit exposure when air quality is bad, by staying indoors or wearing a mask. This is not always possible, though. Danny Djarum is with the World Resources Institute. He told the AP there are many people who live or work outside and “can’t really afford” to stay indoors.

While air purifiers can help reduce indoor air pollution, experts say they do have limitations. The devices work by pulling air from a room and then pushing it through a filter that traps pollutants. The filtered air is then sent back into the room.

Air purifiers work best when used in small spaces and when people are nearby. This is because they can only clean a certain amount of air, said Rajasekhar Balasubramanian of the National University of Singapore. He added, “If we have a tiny air purifier in a large room, it won’t be effective.”
titulo_es: How to reduce the risks of bad air quality
resumen_es: Air pollution affects almost the entire world population and causes about seven million deaths a year; the text explains its sources, its effects on health, how to read air quality indexes and what people can do to protect themselves.

ideas_clave.idea: Almost the entire world population breathes air that at times exceeds WHO limits, and pollution kills around seven million people a year, though individuals can take steps to protect themselves.
Air can be polluted even when it does not look smoky; most pollutants come from burning fuels, crops or forests, and from wildfires.
The most harmful pollutants include fine particles such as PM 2.5, which penetrate deep into the lungs, and gases like nitrogen and sulfur dioxide, mainly produced by combustion.

Exposure causes asthma, heart attacks, strokes and long-term heart and lung disease, and in East Asia and the Pacific it affects hundreds of millions of children, killing about 100 young children daily.
Thousands of cities monitor air quality and many countries use an index to make the data understandable, but national standards vary widely, India's being much laxer than the WHO's.
Experts recommend limiting exposure by staying indoors or wearing masks, although many outdoor workers cannot afford to do so.
Air purifiers can reduce indoor pollution by filtering air, but they are only effective in small spaces and close to people.

resumen_modelo: The text warns that nearly everyone in the world is exposed at some point to air that fails to meet WHO standards, and that pollution causes around seven million deaths a year. Pollution is not always visible: it mainly results from burning fuels, crops or forests and from wildfires. The most dangerous pollutants are fine particles, which reach deep into the lungs, and gases such as nitrogen and sulfur dioxide. In the short term they can trigger asthma, heart attacks and strokes, whereas long-term exposure may cause fatal heart and lung diseases; children are especially vulnerable, particularly in East Asia. Although many cities now measure air quality and many countries use an index to simplify the figures, national standards differ considerably. Experts therefore advise limiting exposure by staying indoors or wearing a mask, even if this is not an option for many outdoor workers, and they point out that air purifiers only work well in small rooms.

preguntas.pregunta: What percentage of the world's population breathes air that does not meet WHO guidelines at some point?
preguntas.cita: about 99 percent of the world’s population breathes air at some point that does not meet pollution guidelines
preguntas.explicacion: The text gives a figure of 99 %. The other figures do not appear.

preguntas.enunciado: Say whether the statement is true, false or not stated in the text.
preguntas.pregunta: According to the WHO, air pollution kills about 7 million people every year.
preguntas.cita: Different forms of air pollution kill about 7 million people each year, the U.N. health agency estimates.
preguntas.explicacion: The UN health agency, that is, the WHO, estimates about seven million deaths a year.

preguntas.enunciado: Say whether the statement is true, false or not stated in the text.
preguntas.pregunta: According to Tanushree Ganguly, air is only polluted when it looks smoky.
preguntas.cita: air is not only polluted when it looks smoky or smoggy
preguntas.explicacion: Ganguly says the opposite: the air can be polluted even if it does not look smoky and there is no smog.

preguntas.enunciado: Find in paragraph 3 a word for forest fires.
preguntas.pregunta: Find a word for large fires that spread in the countryside or forests.
preguntas.cita: Pollutants can also be released from wildfires.
preguntas.explicacion: “Wildfires” are uncontrolled fires in the countryside or forests; also “forest fires” or “bushfires”.

preguntas.pregunta: What is PM 2.5 mainly created by?
preguntas.cita: These particles can travel deep inside human lungs and are mostly created by burning fuels.
preguntas.explicacion: PM 2.5 come mainly from burning fuels. Agriculture, windblown dust and mining are associated with the larger particles, PM 10.

preguntas.enunciado: Find in paragraph 6 a word for a sudden interruption of blood supply to the brain.
preguntas.pregunta: Find the word for a sudden interruption of blood supply to the brain.
preguntas.cita: increase the risk of heart attacks and stroke
preguntas.explicacion: A “stroke” (es: ictus, derrame cerebral); a “heart attack” (es: infarto).

preguntas.pregunta: What is the difference between the effects of short-term and long-term exposure to air pollution?
respuestas: Short-term exposure can trigger asthma attacks and raise the risk of heart attacks and strokes, especially in older or ill people, whereas long-term exposure can cause serious heart and lung diseases that may be fatal.
preguntas.cita: Long-term exposure can cause serious heart and lung problems that can lead to death.
preguntas.explicacion: The answer must contrast the acute effects (asthma, heart attacks, strokes in vulnerable people) with the chronic ones (potentially fatal heart and lung diseases).

preguntas.pregunta: According to UNICEF, how many children under 5 die every day from pollution-linked causes in East Asia and the Pacific?
preguntas.cita: The pollution is linked to the deaths of 100 children under age 5 every day.
preguntas.explicacion: It is about 100 deaths a day. The 500 million are the children who breathe unhealthy air and 6,000 is the number of cities that measure air quality.

preguntas.enunciado: Say whether the statement is true, false or not stated in the text.
preguntas.pregunta: On an air quality index, larger numbers mean better air.
preguntas.cita: Larger numbers on this index mean worse air.
preguntas.explicacion: It is the other way round: the higher the index, the worse the air quality.

preguntas.pregunta: How does India's daily PM 2.5 limit compare with WHO standards?
preguntas.cita: India’s daily PM 2.5 limit is more than 1.5 times higher than in Thailand and 4 times higher than WHO standards.
preguntas.explicacion: The Indian limit is four times the WHO limit. The figure of 1.5 times refers to the comparison with Thailand.

preguntas.enunciado: Say whether the statement is true, false or not stated in the text.
preguntas.pregunta: The European Union has the strictest air quality standards in the world.
preguntas.explicacion: The text only compares India, Thailand and the WHO; it does not mention the European Union.

preguntas.pregunta: Why is the advice to stay indoors when air quality is bad not equally useful for everyone?
respuestas: Because many people live or work outdoors and cannot afford to stay inside, so the poorest and outdoor workers remain exposed even when they know the air is dangerous.
preguntas.cita: there are many people who live or work outside and “can’t really afford” to stay indoors
preguntas.explicacion: An inference question about inequality in exposure to pollution: being able to protect yourself depends on your economic and work situation.
